title.en: Itzamna, the Priest Who Named Everything
title.zh: 伊察姆納：為萬物命名的大祭司

region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦伊扎馬爾

source.work: Diego de Landa, Relacion de las cosas de Yucatan, trans. Alfred M. Tozzer (1941); Fray Bernardo de Lizana, Devocionario (1633)

texts.license: Landa's sixteenth-century text public domain; Tozzer translation copyrighted and only paraphrased

summary.en: Itzamna — called Zamna, 'the lizard house', god of the heavens and of day and night — was the priest of the gods: he invented letters, the calendar, and the count of days, gave each thing its name, and healed the sick without payment. At Izamal his temple was the greatest of the land, and the pilgrims of the old religion came there as to Rome and Jerusalem.
summary.zh: 伊察姆納——又稱扎姆納，意為「蜥之家」，天空之神、晝夜之主——是諸神的大祭司：他發明文字、曆法與日數，為萬物命名，並不取分文地醫治病人。伊扎馬爾的神廟為全地之最，舊教朝聖者視之如羅馬與耶路撒冷。

sensitivity.note: Sixteenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of published translations only.

passages.text: The Yucatec held Itzamna to be a god of the heavens, the maker and lord of day and of night, and the priest of their gods in the time of the ancients: it was he who gave each thing its name, and who taught them the letters, the count of the years, months and days, and the feasts and ceremonies that go with the count.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion, sections on the gods (Tozzer trans. 1941); not verbatim.

passages.text: He was so devoted to his people that he healed them, they say, of every sickness, and never asked a fee: medicine and writing and the calendar came to them as gifts. Because of this they built him the temple at Izamal, and made roads to it from all the ends of the land, so that all the province came to worship there as the Christians to Rome.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Lizana, Devocionario (1633), on Zamna and Izamal (Tozzer ed. 1941); not verbatim.

texts.language: Sixteenth-century Spanish record of Yucatec tradition
texts.canonical_translation: Tozzer, Landa's Relacion (1941); Lizana trans. via Tozzer notes

narrative.en:
Diego de Landa, writing about 1566, records that the Yucatec worshipped as a principal god Itzamna, whom they called also Zamna, the 'house of the lizard', a god of the heavens who had been the priest of the gods in the time of the ancients. It was Itzamna who gave names to the rivers, the places, and the things of the world; who invented the letters and the books; and who worked out the calendar — the count of the years, months, days, and feasts — teaching it to the priests who came after him. His cult center was Izamal, where the great pyramids of the town were said to be his, and Lizana, writing in 1633 from local memory, adds the detail that Zamna healed the sick of every illness and never asked a fee, and that four great roads were made from the ends of the land to his temple, as causeways to Rome and Jerusalem are made for pilgrims.

The Itzamna record is the Maya culture-hero cycle of Yucatán: a founder who is at once god, priest, physician, and civilizer. His healing without payment marks him as a god of free grace, unlike the priced covenants of Tohil in the highlands; his invention of writing and of the calendar marks him as the patron of the Ah Kin, the day-priests, whose title means literally 'he of the sun'; and his naming of everything echoes the Popol Wuj's creation by word — in Yucatán, the power of naming is remembered as the gift of a god who walked among the people.

At Izamal the memory of Itzamna is fused with that of Kinich Kakmó, 'the sun-faced', an idol which had its temple on the highest mound of the city, where from the top the sea itself could be seen. Landa's contemporaries reported the founders of Izamal as figures named Kinich Kabul, Kinich Kakmo, Cit Ah Cutz, and Cit Ah Coyi — 'father of the turkey lineage' and 'father of the coyote lineage' — founder-gods whose names became the patronymics of living families. Ritual function: Izamal remained the pilgrimage center of Yucatán under colonial rule; the Franciscans deliberately built their monastery on Itzamna's platform (1549), converting the god's own geography into Christian space while the roads of the god continued to carry pilgrims.

For the comparative study of culture heroes, Itzamna belongs beside Osiris, Thoth, and Quetzalcoatl: the god who gives writing, calendar, and medicine as a single civilizing gift. His Yucatec specificity lies in the way the gift is staged - naming. To give a thing its name, in the Maya world, is to bring it into the count of days; and Itzamna is remembered as the first counter, the priest whose naming made the calendar possible. The survival of his name into the Lacandon pantheon (Ioana, the caretaker of the underworld, as Tozzer found it in 1907) shows how long the office of the naming priest remained a living institution.

functions: Culture-hero charter of writing, calendar, and healing in Yucatán
Explains the sacred geography of Izamal as pilgrimage center with roads from all quarters
Authorizes the Ah Kin priesthood as heirs of the god's own office

variants.text_tradition: Lizana, Devocionario de Ntra. Sra. de Izamal (1633)
variants.summary: Local Izamal memory makes Zamna the healer and road-maker; Landa's version stresses invention of letters and calendar.

title.en: Kukulcan, the Feathered Serpent, Comes from the West
title.zh: 羽蛇庫庫爾坎自西方而來

region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦奇琴伊察

source.work: Diego de Landa, Relacion de las cosas de Yucatan, trans. Alfred M. Tozzer (1941); Antonio de Herrera, Historia General (1601-15)

texts.license: Sixteenth-century texts public domain; Tozzer translation only paraphrased

summary.en: At Chichen Itza there reigned a great lord called Kukulcan — a man of good ability, without wife or children, public-spirited, and therefore considered a god. Whether he came before, after, or with the Itzas none agreed; but he ruled in peace, and after his return to Mexico he was worshipped there as Quetzalcoatl.
summary.zh: 奇琴伊察曾有一位偉大的君主庫庫爾坎——才幹出眾，無妻無子，熱心公益，因此被視為神。其到來早於、晚於抑或伴隨伊察人，眾說不一；但他治世以和平；回墨西哥之後，即被尊為羽蛇神克薩爾科亞特爾。

sensitivity.note: Sixteenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of published translations only.

passages.text: Among them there is a belief that a great lord called Kukulcan reigned, and all agree that he entered from the direction of the west; the difference of opinion which exists concerning this is only whether he entered before or after the Itzas or with them. He was a man of good ability; he had no wife nor children; he was very public-spirited and for this reason considered a god.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Herrera, Historia General (1601-15), Appendix A (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

passages.text: They say that he was favorably disposed, and that after his return he was regarded in Mexico as one of their gods and called Quetzalcouatl; and they also considered him a god in Yucatan, because of his great virtues and his gentleness. It is said he taught them, and that a beautiful building was dedicated to his name at Chichen Itza, with the serpent of the balustrade, by which his arrival was remembered.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion, on Kukulcan (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

title.en: Kukulcan Builds the Walled City of Mayapan
title.zh: 庫庫爾坎築牆城馬雅潘

source.work: Diego de Landa, Relacion de las cosas de Yucatan, trans. Alfred M. Tozzer (1941); Antonio de Herrera, Historia General (1601-15)

texts.license: Sixteenth-century texts public domain; Tozzer translation only paraphrased

summary.en: To quiet the country, Kukulcan agrees that a new city should be founded where all affairs could go. Eight leagues inland from Merida they built a circle of dry stone wall with only two doors, raised the temples, named the largest for Kukulcan, and divided the land among the lords — the beginning of the government of Mayapan.
summary.zh: 為平定邦國，庫庫爾坎議定另建一城，使諸務皆歸於此。眾人在梅里達城址以內八里格處，築乾砌石牆圓城，僅開兩門；建諸神廟，最大者以庫庫爾坎為名，並將土地分予諸侯——馬雅潘政權由此而始。

sensitivity.note: Sixteenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of published translations only.

passages.text: In order to tranquillize the country he agreed to found another city where all affairs should go. They chose a site for this eight leagues further inland from where the city of Merida now is and fifteen from the sea, and there they made a circle of about an eighth of a league consisting of a wall in stone laid dry, leaving only two doors.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Herrera, Historia General (1601-15), Appendix A (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

passages.text: They made their temples and called the largest Kukulcan, and they also built the houses of the lords near the enclosure. Kukulcan divided the land among the latter, and the city was called Mayapan; and in this way peace returned and the government endured in that place for many generations, until the tyrant Cocom brought ruin on it.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

title.en: The Three Brothers of Chichen Itza

region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦奇琴伊察

source.work: Diego de Landa, Relacion de las cosas de Yucatan, trans. Alfred M. Tozzer (1941)

texts.license: Sixteenth-century texts public domain; Tozzer translation only paraphrased

summary.en: Chichen Itza was ruled, they say, by three lordly brothers who came from the west and lived very chastely with their wives; they built the great temples. But when one of them died, the other two began to act unjustly and indecently; the people hated them, put them to death, and abandoned the place and its buildings.
summary.zh: 據言奇琴伊察由三位自西方而來的君王兄弟共治，其妻皆守貞潔；他們建造了宏偉的神廟。然而其中一人死後，其餘二人開始行事不義不端；民眾惡之，遂誅二人，棄城而去，連其偉大建築也一併拋下。

sensitivity.note: Sixteenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of published translations only.

passages.text: It is said that Chichen Itza was ruled by three lords who were brothers, who came into that country from the west; they were very devout, and they built very beautiful temples, and their wives lived very chastely. One of them died or went away, upon which the other two acted unjustly and indecently, and for this they were put to death.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

passages.text: In time, they say, one of them died, and his absence left so great a flaw that the other two began to be dishonest and partial, and to such a degree that the people hated them; so they killed them and abandoned the place and left the buildings, especially the most honorable, which is ten leagues from the sea. Those who settled Chichen Itza are called the Itzas.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Herrera, Historia General, Appendix A (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

title.en: Governor Cocom Covets Riches: The Mexicans Enter Mayapan
title.zh: 科科姆總督貪財：墨西哥人入馬雅潘

texts.period: Recorded c. 1566 (Landa); events of the 13th-15th c.; Tozzer edition 1941

source.work: Diego de Landa, Relacion de las cosas de Yucatan, trans. Alfred M. Tozzer (1941)

texts.license: Sixteenth-century texts public domain; Tozzer translation only paraphrased

summary.en: Governor Cocom begins to covet riches and arranges with the Mexican garrisons kept at Tabasco and Xicalango to hand over his city. The Mexican troops enter Mayapan, the governor oppresses the poor and makes slaves — the first to do so, the record insists — and the Yucatecans, learning the use of the bow, the lance and the axe, cease to fear them.
summary.zh: 科科姆總督起貪財之心，與墨西哥人在塔巴斯科與希卡蘭戈的衛戍部隊相約，欲將其城交出。墨西哥軍入馬雅潘，總督欺凌貧民、役使奴隸——史載此為奴役之始——而猶加敦人習得弓、矛、斧之用，自此不再畏懼他們。

sensitivity.note: Sixteenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of published translations only.

passages.text: The Governor Cocom began to covet riches, and for this reason he arranged with the troops of the garrison which the kings of Mexico kept at Tabasco and Xicalango to hand over the city to them. And thus he brought the Mexican people into Mayapan, and oppressed the poor and made many slaves; and the lords would have put him to death but for the fear which they had of the Mexicans.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

passages.text: The lord of the Tutul Xius never consented to this. And the Yucatecans, finding themselves in this situation, learned from the Mexicans the use of arms, and they soon became masters of the bow and arrow, the lance and the axe, their shields and jackets made strong with cotton, so that finally they neither admired the Mexicans nor feared them, but took little account of them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fall of Mayapan: Tyranny and the Absent Son
title.zh: 馬雅潘之傾覆：暴政與倖存的獨子

texts.period: Recorded c. 1566 (Landa); fall c. 1441-60; Tozzer edition 1941

source.work: Diego de Landa, Relacion de las cosas de Yucatan, trans. Alfred M. Tozzer (1941)

texts.license: Sixteenth-century texts public domain; Tozzer translation only paraphrased

summary.en: A haughty successor of Cocom's house makes a second league with Tabasco, introduces more Mexicans, and plays the tyrant, enslaving the poor. The nobles join the just Tutul Xiu, conspire against Cocom, kill him and all his sons but one who is absent, sack his house, and take back his lands — and after five hundred years of dwelling there, the parties abandon Mayapan, each returning to his own country.
summary.zh: 科科姆家族的繼任者傲慢仿其先人，再與塔巴斯科結盟，引入更多墨西哥人，行暴政而奴役貧民。諸侯遂擁公正的圖圖爾·希烏，密謀誅科科姆——殺其與其諸子，唯獨缺席的一子倖免；劫其家，奪其可可田與果園以償所奪。城居五百餘年之後，各方棄城而去，各歸其國。

sensitivity.note: Sixteenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of published translations only.

passages.text: Among the successors of the house of Cocom was a very haughty man, an imitator of Cocom, and he made another league with the men of Tabasco, and he introduced more Mexicans into the city, and he began to play the tyrant and to make slaves of the poorer people. On this account the nobles joined with the party of Tutul Xiu, who was a just statesman like his ancestors, and they conspired to put Cocom to death.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

passages.text: This they did, killing at the same time all his sons, except one who was absent. They sacked his house and took away the lands which he had in cacao and in other fruits, saying that they paid themselves for what he had taken from them. The quarrels between the Cocoms, who said they had been unjustly expelled, and the Xius lasted so long that after they had lived in that city for more than five hundred years, they abandoned it and left it in solitude, each party returning to his own country.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

title.en: The Well of Chichen: Living Men, Precious Stones, and the Voice from Below
title.zh: 奇琴之井：活人、寶石與井下之聲

region.en: Sacred Cenote of Chichen Itza, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦奇琴伊察聖井

source.work: Diego de Landa, Relacion de las cosas de Yucatan, trans. Alfred M. Tozzer (1941)

texts.license: Sixteenth-century texts public domain; Tozzer translation only paraphrased

summary.en: From a paved causeway running from the court of the great building, a well opens in the living rock, green with the groves around it. Into it, in times of drought, they threw living men as sacrifice, believing they did not die though they never saw them again; with them precious stones and things they prized, gold cup and bowl, so great was their devotion. If the country had had gold, they say, all of it would be in that well.
summary.zh: 自大神殿前庭有一石鋪大道，通往岩層中天然開口的深井，井水因四圍林木而呈綠色。大旱之時，人們將活人投入井中獻祭，堅信其人未死、只是不再被人看見；同投者有寶石與珍愛之物、金杯與金碗，奉獻之誠如此。人言：若此地有金，皆在井中。

sensitivity.note: Sixteenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of published translations only.

passages.text: From the court in front of these stages a wide and handsome causeway runs as far as a well which is about two stones' throw off. Into this well they have had, and then had, the custom of throwing men alive as a sacrifice to the gods in times of drought, and they believed that they did not die though they never saw them again.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

passages.text: They also threw into it a great many other things, like precious stones and things which they prized. And so, if this country had possessed gold, it would be this well that would have the greater part of it, so great was the devotion which the Indians showed for it. The well is more than seven stadia deep down to the water, and more than one hundred feet broad, marvellously formed by a circular and perpendicular opening in the living rock, and the water appears green, which they say is caused by the groves with which it is surrounded.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

texts.language: Sixteenth-century Spanish record of Yucatec practice

narrative.en:
Landa's description of the Sacred Cenote is the classic colonial account of Maya pilgrimage sacrifice. A wide paved causeway (the sacbe still traceable today) runs from the great pyramid's court northward to a natural well — the cenote — cut by a circular perpendicular opening in the living rock, more than a hundred feet across, its water green from the groves around it. Into this well, Landa records, the Yucatec 'have had, and then had', the custom of throwing living men as sacrifice to the gods in time of drought, believing that they did not die though they were never seen again; with the victims went precious stones, cups of gold, bowls, and everything they prized — so much so, Landa observes, that if the country had possessed gold, the greater part of it would have been at the bottom of that well.

The rite was divinatory as much as propitiatory. The Relacion of Valladolid (recorded in Tozzer's notes from the 1580s) describes the full procedure: the lords of all the provinces fasted sixty days without raising their eyes to their wives or to those who brought them food; at break of dawn they threw into the well Indian women who had been told to ask the gods for a good year; at exactly midday the one who was to come out shouted for a rope, and when she was drawn up half-dead, great fires were made around her and she was censed with copal. Revived, she reported that many of her race were below, men as well as women, who received her, and that when she raised her head they struck her neck so that she would keep it bowed. She answered their questions — good year or bad — and if the demon was angry with a lord, his woman did not ask to be taken out at noon, and never came out.

The 1562 idolatry testimonies taken under Landa's own inquisition add a village-level echo: messengers carried a boy to Chichen, threw him into the cenote, waited a day to hear 'the reply of what their gods had told him' about pestilence or food or sterility, and, when he did not come out, returned to report. And a post-conquest episode — the Xiu pilgrimage for rain, with its Cocamb ambush — shows the well still commanding the politics of the peninsula long after the conquest had begun.

Archaeologically, Edward H. Thompson's dredging (1904-10) recovered the gold and copper bells, jade beads, carved plaques, wooden objects, human bones, and copal balls that verify the accounts. The well's cultural function is threefold: it is an oracle (the victim returns with the year's answer), a covenant of rain (drought victims, boys and girls, sent to speak with the rain gods), and a treasury of the community's wealth surrendered to the water. In Maya cosmology the cenote is an entrance to the watery underworld — Xibalba's channels — and the sacrifice at noon (midday, the hour of the divinatory return) marks the axis between the living town and the dead water.

functions: Rain covenant in drought: living victims sent to petition the water gods
Oracle: the survivor returns at noon with the year's answer
Community treasury: gold, jade, and prized goods surrendered to the water

variants.text_tradition: Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel (Roys 1933)

texts.sensitivity_guidance: The cenote is still a living sacred site for some Maya communities; describe rites historically, avoid sensationalizing the victims, and note that modern Maya people visit and revere the place.

title.en: The Xius Walk to the Well and Are Burned on the Road
title.zh: 希烏人朝聖於井，途中遭焚

region.en: Road from Mani to Chichen Itza, Yucatan, Mexico
region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦自馬尼往奇琴伊察之路

texts.period: Recorded c. 1566 (Landa); events of the 1550s-60s; Tozzer edition 1941

source.work: Diego de Landa, Relacion de las cosas de Yucatan, trans. Alfred M. Tozzer (1941)

texts.license: Sixteenth-century texts public domain; Tozzer translation only paraphrased

summary.en: Rain fails in the whole land and there is famine; the lords of Mani, of the Xiu lineage, agree on a solemn sacrifice and take male and female slaves to throw into the well of Chichen Itza. To reach it they must pass through Cocom country; the Cocoms, wanting vengeance, let them pass — then burn the pilgrims alive and shoot down those who flee.
summary.zh: 全地無雨，饑饉大作；馬尼的希烏族君長議定行莊嚴之祭，攜男女奴隸投入奇琴伊察之井。前往之路必經科科姆之地；懷恨已久的科科姆人表面允其通行——旋即將朝聖者活活燒死，以箭射殺逃脫者。

sensitivity.note: Sixteenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of published translations only.

passages.text: Rain being lacking in the whole land, little bread was gathered, and they came to such great extremity that they ate barks of trees. As a result of this famine the lords of Mani, who are those of the Xiu lineage, agreed to make a solemn sacrifice to the idols, and taking certain male and female slaves in order to throw them into the well of Chichen Itza.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

passages.text: It was necessary to pass through the pueblo of those of the Cocom lineage, their ancient and capital enemies; and not believing that they would renew the old passions at such a time, they sent to them to give an account of their journey and ask to be allowed to pass. The Cocoms, who were desirous of avenging ancient injuries, cautiously replied all right, they might go. Having reached a pueblo two leagues from Cocom, they lodged in a large house, where the Cocoms set fire to them and burned them, and shot with arrows those who escaped.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

title.en: The Five Unlucky Days: The Bacabs at the Four Entrances of the Town
title.zh: 五個凶日：鎮口四方的巴卡布

source.work: Diego de Landa, Relacion de las cosas de Yucatan, trans. Alfred M. Tozzer (1941)

texts.license: Sixteenth-century texts public domain; Tozzer translation only paraphrased

summary.en: For the New Year the Maya used the five unlucky days before the first of Pop. In the Kan year, whose omen is Hobnil of the south, they made a hollow figure of clay called Kan u Uayeyab, set it on a heap of stones at the southern entrance of the town, and raised the statue of Bolon Dzacab in the chief's house; the priest and lords assemble, chase out the evil spirit, pierce ears and tongues, anoint the idols, and so begin the year.
summary.zh: 歲首之祭用一月波普之前的五個凶日。坎年之兆為南方之霍布尼爾；眾人塑名為坎·烏·瓦耶亞布的黏土空心神像，置於鎮南入口的石堆之上，並在酋長家中立起博倫·察卡布之神像；祭司與諸侯齊聚，驅逐惡靈，穿耳穿舌，塗聖諸像，然後歲曆更新。

sensitivity.note: Sixteenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of published translations only.

passages.text: For celebrating the festival of the New Year, this people, with great rejoicing and with much dignity according to their unhappy ideas, made use of the five unlucky days which were regarded by them as such before the first day of the new year. In these days they held many services for the Bacabs and for the gods called Kan u Uayeyab, Chac u Uayeyab, Sac u Uayeyab and Ek u Uayeyab.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

passages.text: It was the custom in all the towns in Yucatan that there should be two heaps of stone facing each other at the entrance of the town on all four sides — east, west, north and south. In the Kan year the omen was Hobnil, and they ruled in the region of the south; they made an image or hollow figure of the god of clay, which they called Kan u Uayeyab, and carried it to the heaps of dry stone raised at the southern side.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

passages.text: They chose a chief of the town in whose house the festival was celebrated, and made the statue of a god called Bolon Dzacab, which they placed in the house of the principal, adorned, in a public place where everyone could go to it. Then the lords, the priest and the men of the town assembled, and they began by chasing away from themselves the evil spirit, in order to perform the ceremony the better — sometimes by prayers and benedictions, at other times by offerings and sacrifices.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

texts.language: Sixteenth-century Spanish record of Yucatec ritual

narrative.en:
Landa's longest ritual description is the set of four New Year ceremonies attached to the four year-bearers of the Yucatec calendar: Kan, Muluc, Ix, and Cauac, each with its color (red east, white north, black west, yellow south), its Bacab, its Pauah Tun, its Xib Chac, and its Uayeyab idol. The ceremonies were held in the five 'unlucky' nameless days (the Uayeb) before the first of Pop, when the old year is dying and the new one must be carried across the threshold.

In each of the four rites the pattern is the same in shape and different in color and direction: two heaps of dry stone face each other at the entrance of the town on the side belonging to the year's color; a hollow figure of baked clay, named for the year (Kan u Uayeyab, and so on), is carried to the stone heaps and seated on the crossbars of green poles; a statue of the year's god (for instance Bolon Dzacab) is set up in the house of the chief chosen to give the feast; the evil spirit is chased away first — by prayers, benedictions, offerings — because no ceremony can proceed while he lingers; and then come the sacrifices. Hearts of quail are burned; the Chacs, the four assistants of the rite, draw blood by piercing tongues and ears with blades, and anoint the idols; the dancers carry the god on a litter to the sound of drum and conch and flute, singing, and drink a wine of fermented bark until they are overcome.

Each year also brings its specific calamities to avert, and Landa lists them: in the Kan year, the south's dominion, the evils are those of the yellow (kan) color; in the Muluc year the omen is Can tzic nal and the direction east; in the Ix year, Sac cimi and the north; in the Cauac year, Hosan ek and the west. The tunkul (split drum), the conch, and the flute give the sound of the transition; the fire, the new idols, and the swept courts give its material form.

As a corpus record this is the Maya counterpart of the New Year renewal clusters in other traditions: the world is renewed by re-coloring it, by re-stationing its gods at the four gates, and by feeding them blood before the calendar turns. The connection to the Dresden Codex pages 25-28 and Tro-Cortesianus 34-37 — which picture the same Uayeb rites — makes this one of the few places where a colonial text, a codex, and living practice (the Cha-chaac rain rites recorded among the modern Maya) describe the same liturgy.

functions: Renewal of time: the year is inaugurated by re-stationing the direction gods at the four gates
Expiation: the evil spirit must be driven off before any ceremony
Blood covenant: tongue and ear piercing with ac-grass blades feeds the year-gods
Links the colonial liturgy to Dresden 25-28 and to modern Cha-chaac rain rites

variants.name: Dresden Codex 25-28 / Tro-Cortesianus 34-37
variants.summary: The codices picture the same Uayeb rites: the year-bearer idols carried on litters, seated on the stone heaps, with the four colors and the offerings.

primary_sources.work: Diego de Landa, Relacion de las cosas de Yucatan
primary_sources.citation: c. 1566; Tozzer trans. 1941, sections on the New Year, pp. 135-42

secondary_sources.work: J. Eric S. Thompson, Maya Hieroglyphic Writing

texts.sensitivity_guidance: The Uayeb renewal logic continues in modern Maya year-turning and Cha-chaac rites; present as historical description of a living liturgical system.

title.en: The Feast of the Hunters: Deer Skulls and Ac Grass

texts.period: Recorded c. 1566 (Landa), month Zip; Tozzer edition 1941

source.work: Diego de Landa, Relacion de las cosas de Yucatan, trans. Alfred M. Tozzer (1941)

texts.license: Sixteenth-century texts public domain; Tozzer translation only paraphrased

summary.en: In the month Zip the hunters' festival is held. The priests drive out the evil spirit, set up the sacrifice apparatus with new fire and blue bitumen, and invoke the gods of the chase. Some dance holding anointed deer skulls and arrows; others pierce their ears and tongues and pass seven wide blades of ac grass through the holes, then pour out the wine until they are overcome.
summary.zh: 希普月行獵人之祭。祭司驅逐惡靈，備祭器、新火與藍色樹脂，召請狩獵諸神。有人執塗聖的鹿首與箭起舞；有人穿耳穿舌，以七片寬茅草葉貫穿孔竅；禮成之後，傾酒痛飲，直至醉倒。

sensitivity.note: Sixteenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of published translations only.

passages.text: The priests came and drove away the evil spirit as usual. After he had been driven out they placed in the middle the apparatus for the sacrifice, incense and new fire, and the blue bitumen. And the hunters devoutly invoked the gods of the chase, Acanum, Suhui Dzip, Tabai and others, and distributed the incense which they threw into the brazier.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

passages.text: While it was burning, each took an arrow and the skull of a deer, which the Chacs anointed with the blue bitumen. And some danced holding these thus anointed in their hands, while others pierced their ears and others their tongues, and passed through the holes seven rather wide blades of a kind of grass called ac. This done, the priest first, and then the officers of the festival, offered the gifts; and so dancing, the wine was poured out, and they got drunk until they were overcome.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fishermen Cut Their Ears and Set Up the Pole

texts.period: Recorded c. 1566 (Landa), month Zec; Tozzer edition 1941

source.work: Diego de Landa, Relacion de las cosas de Yucatan, trans. Alfred M. Tozzer (1941)

texts.license: Sixteenth-century texts public domain; Tozzer translation only paraphrased

summary.en: The day after the hunters, the fishermen celebrate their feast: they anoint their fishing implements, cut their ears round the edges instead of piercing them, dance the Chohom, bless a tall thick pole and set it upright — and then the lords go to the shore with a great company to catch fish with rejoicing.
summary.zh: 獵祭次日，漁人行其祭：他們塗聖漁具，不以穿孔而沿耳緣割切，跳卓霍姆之舞，祝聖一根粗高的木柱而立之——然後君長們率大隊人馬前往海濱，歡騰捕魚。

sensitivity.note: Sixteenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of published translations only.

passages.text: At once on the following day the fishermen celebrated the festival in the same way as the others, except that the things which they anointed were their fishing implements, and they did not pierce their ears, but they cut them round the edges, and they danced a dance called Chohom.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

passages.text: When all this was done, they blessed a tall and thick pole, and set it upright. When this festival was ended in the towns, the lords were accustomed to go to celebrate it with a large number of people on the shore, where they caught a large number of fish with rejoicings, carrying a large supply of trammel nets, hooks and other instruments for fishing.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Landa, Relacion (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦伊扎馬爾

source.work: Diego de Landa, Relacion de las cosas de Yucatan, trans. Alfred M. Tozzer (1941); Lizana, Devocionario (1633)

texts.license: Sixteenth-century texts public domain; Tozzer translation only paraphrased

summary.en: On the highest mound of Izamal stood the temple of Kinich Kakmó, 'the sun with a face'. The first inhabitants of the city were remembered as founder-gods — Kinich Kabul, Kinich Kakmo, Cit Ah Cutz ('father of the turkey lineage'), Cit Ah Coyi ('father of the coyote lineage') — whose names became the patronymics of living families. From the temple's top one saw the whole land and the sea.
summary.zh: 伊扎馬爾最高的丘上，立有基尼奇·卡克莫——「有面之日」——的神廟。城中初民被記為創族之神：基尼奇·卡布爾、基尼奇·卡克莫、西特·阿·庫茨（火雞氏之父）、西特·阿·科伊（郊狼氏之父），其名成為後世家族的姓氏。自廟頂可望全境與大海。

sensitivity.note: Sixteenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of published translations only.

passages.text: There was also another mound at Izamal which is today the highest one, and it is called Kinich Kakmo, the reason being that there was a temple on top of it and in it an idol which had this name, which in our language means 'the sun with a face'. From the top of the chapel one sees wonderfully well, as far as the sight can reach, and the sea is visible.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Lizana, Devocionario (1633), and Landa (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.

passages.text: The first inhabitants of the city were Kinich Kabul, Kinich Kakmo, Cit Ah Cutz and Cit Ah Coyi, from whom descended the Xols, the Mos and the Coyes. These first inhabitants should be considered founder gods: their names became the surnames of the lineages that still bear them, so that the god of the sun-faced temple is also the ancestor in the count of families.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Relacion of Izamal and Lizana (Tozzer 1941); not verbatim.
